screens.title: Understanding the Threat Landscape: Actors, Vectors, and Motivations
screens.narratorSegment: To defend effectively, you must first understand the people and methods behind attacks. In this lesson you will build a mental model for classifying threat actors — from casual script kiddies to sophisticated advanced persistent threats — and learn the common vectors they use, such as phishing, malware, and web application exploitation. You will also learn how attacker motivations, whether financial, political, or opportunistic, shape what they target and when they act. Finally, we will introduce the MITRE ATT&CK framework as a practical language for mapping adversary behavior to tactics and techniques. This orientation matters because detection and response choices change when you know the likely adversary and their motives. For example, an incident that looks like credential theft from a phishing email will be triaged differently if you suspect a nation-state espionage group versus a financially motivated gang. By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify actor categories, link them to likely vectors, and begin mapping observed activity to ATT&CK techniques so you can prioritize investigations and recommend mitigations. Consider what pattern of behavior would make you treat an alert as urgent versus informational.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Classifying threat actors and understanding their preferred vectors and motivations lets analysts prioritize alerts, tailor hunting, and map incidents to MITRE ATT&CK for consistent investigations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Overview
Understanding the Threat Landscape
Who attacks your systems, the methods they use, and the motives that drive them.
Why this matters

Classification helps you prioritize: attacks with high capability and targeted motives demand faster, deeper response than low-skill opportunistic probing.

How you'll use it

Map alerts to actor profiles and ATT&CK techniques to choose triage level, hunt queries, and control hardening recommendations.

Explore Key Topics
Actors
Script kiddies to APTs — capability and intent guide response.
Vectors
Phishing, malware, DDoS, and web vulnerabilities are common entry paths.
Motivations
Financial, espionage, political, revenge, and notoriety shape targets.
Threat Overview Visual
16:9 Masterclass
Actors
  • Script kiddie — low skill, notoriety
  • Hacktivist — ideological targets
  • Organized crime — financial motive
  • APT — espionage, long game
Vectors & Motives
  • Phishing / spear phishing — credential theft
  • Malware — compromise & persistence
  • Web vulnerabilities — data exfiltration
  • Motives: money, espionage, politics
Quick Start
As you proceed, notice how actor capability changes the urgency of alerts and how ATT&CK gives you a consistent taxonomy to search for attacker techniques.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to categorize threat actors by capability and intent, identify common attack vectors, explain attacker motivations, and apply the MITRE ATT&CK framework to real incidents. First, you will learn to distinguish simple attackers who use off‑the‑shelf tools from sophisticated, well‑resourced groups whose goals are espionage or infrastructure disruption. Second, you will map vectors such as phishing, malware delivery, DDoS, and web application exploits to likely outcomes so you can recognize early indicators. Third, you will reason from motivation — for example, understanding that financially motivated groups prioritize data capable of monetization — and use that insight to prioritize. Finally, you will learn to read ATT&CK tactics and techniques and use them to frame hunt queries and incident timelines. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify what you have learned by mapping a scenario to ATT&CK entries and selecting appropriate mitigations. These skills matter because they make your detection more accurate and your response more effective. Think about a recent alert you investigated: which of these objectives would have changed how you triaged it?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page focuses on observable outcomes you should demonstrate after practice. You will learn to extract indicators that point to specific vectors: for example, how suspicious mail headers, unusual referral domains, and credential use patterns signal phishing followed by account misuse. You will practice mapping scenario steps to ATT&CK technique IDs so your investigation reports use a consistent taxonomy. You will also learn to prioritize alerts: treat activity from high-capability actors and those aligned to espionage or infrastructure disruption as high priority, while low-skill opportunistic probes may be monitored until additional evidence appears. A common misconception is to equate volume with severity; a low-volume, targeted intrusion from a sophisticated actor can be more dangerous than a high-volume noisy scan. Practical verification includes mapping a phishing-to-data-access scenario to at least three ATT&CK techniques and explaining why each technique applies. These outcomes align with CySA+ objectives and will improve your detection accuracy and decision-making when incidents arise.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Practical Outcomes
Practical Outcomes
Indicator Extraction
Pull mail headers, sender domains, and attachment hashes to confirm phishing and pivot evidence.

Prioritization
Use actor capability and motivation to set triage levels; avoid volume-only decisions.

screens.title: Threat Actor Categories
screens.narratorSegment: Threat actors are individuals or groups who carry out cyberattacks, and classifying them helps you anticipate method and motive. At the low end you have script kiddies: unsophisticated users who run pre-built tools to exploit known weaknesses, often seeking recognition rather than strategic gain. Hacktivists are ideologically motivated and select symbolic targets to make a statement or disrupt visibility. Organized crime groups are financially driven; they adopt professional practices like ransomware campaigns, data theft, and resale of stolen data, and often have processes resembling a business. Advanced Persistent Threats, or APTs, are highly resourced groups—sometimes nation-state sponsored—with long-term objectives such as espionage or critical infrastructure disruption; they use custom tools and remain stealthy for extended periods. Insider threats are different because they originate from someone with authorized access; harm may be intentional or due to negligence. A useful example: an alert showing a low-skill defacement of a public blog likely indicates a script kiddie, whereas covert exfiltration of R&D from privileged accounts suggests an APT. A common misconception is to treat all breaches the same; in reality, your containment, evidence preservation, and notification decisions should reflect the actor profile. What indicators would make you suspect an insider versus an external actor?

keyIdea.title: Defining Actors
keyIdea.text: Actor classification ranges from low-skill script kiddies to sophisticated APTs and includes insiders; each class implies different detection and response priorities.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Threat Actor Categories
Actor Definitions
Script Kiddie
Beginners using pre-built tools for notoriety. Low sophistication, known tools.
Hacktivist
Ideological motives; symbolic targets chosen to maximize publicity or protest.
Organized Crime
Financially motivated groups with operational practices for extortion and resale.
Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)
Highly resourced, patient, and stealthy groups pursuing long-term objectives like espionage.
Insider Threat
Authorized users who misuse access intentionally or negligently; can be harder to detect.
Example & Analysis
Scenario Comparison
  • Public blog defacement: low skill, noisy — likely script kiddie.
  • Credential harvest then VPN access: targeted, stealthy — could indicate APT or organized crime depending on motive.
  • Privileged employee exfiltrating files: potential insider; examine access logs and HR context.
Key Takeaway

Actor capability and motive change which signals you trust and which containment steps you take.

Common Mistake
Treating all breaches equally. Severity should reflect actor capability and objective, not just event volume.

screens.title: Script Kiddies vs. Hacktivists
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the differences between script kiddies and hacktivists helps you decide how much effort to invest in containment and follow-up. Script kiddies are typically curious or seeking notoriety; they use publicly available tools and target low-hanging fruit such as poorly secured blogs or consumer devices. Their activity tends to be noisy and opportunistic, and indicators include well-known exploit signatures, repeated scanning, and generic payloads. Hacktivists are motivated by ideology. Their attacks are chosen for symbolic impact and may focus on government sites or corporations linked to particular causes; they might also deface pages or leak documents to gain attention. Although hacktivists are not always highly sophisticated, their motives can lead to targeted timing or social-engineering that increases impact. A practical example: a visible defacement on a public website is likely a hacktivist or script kiddie depending on messaging — ideological slogans point to hacktivism, while random brags suggest a script kiddie. A misconception is assuming all ideological attacks are low skill; some hacktivist operations use careful reconnaissance and timing. When you spot early signs like unique slogans or targeted timing, escalate your analysis to look for coordinated messaging and wider campaign indicators. How would your log search change if you suspected ideological motives?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Script Kiddies vs Hacktivists
Profile Comparison
Script Kiddie
  • Motivation: notoriety or mischief
  • Capability: low; pre-made tools
  • Targets: easy public services, blogs
  • Indicators: common payloads, rapid noisy scans
Hacktivist
  • Motivation: political or social agenda
  • Capability: variable; may be targeted
  • Targets: symbolic organizations and services
  • Indicators: defacement messages, timing aligned with events
Concrete Example
Defacement Case
If the defacement contains political slogans and is timed with a protest, treat the activity as hacktivism and search for wider disclosure. If the page simply shows bragging text with reused exploit signatures, it is more likely a script kiddie.
Pro Tip

Use message content and campaign timing as early indicators of ideological intent.

Check Your Understanding
List three observable differences you would search for to distinguish a script kiddie from a hacktivist incident.

screens.title: Organized Crime and APTs
screens.narratorSegment: Organized crime and APTs differ in motive and often in methods, but both can be highly capable and dangerous. Organized crime groups are primarily financially motivated. They develop operations to monetize stolen data, run ransomware campaigns, or sell access. Their activity is often pragmatic: repeatable processes, supply chains for crimeware, and a focus on return on investment. APTs, on the other hand, are frequently sponsored by nation-states or extremely well‑resourced organizations. Their objectives include espionage, intellectual property theft, or disruption of critical infrastructure. APT campaigns are characterized by patient reconnaissance, use of zero-day exploits or bespoke malware, and long-term persistence. A concrete example: an incident that shows staged credential harvesting followed by quiet lateral movement aimed at specific research databases suggests APT activity, while mass ransomware deployment across many victims points to organized crime. A common misconception is that APTs always use exotic tools; sometimes they blend commodity malware with custom tooling and careful operational security. Your response differs: APT suspicion demands comprehensive evidence preservation, intelligence sharing, and a broader hunt for lateral activity. Ask yourself: what signs would convince you that an intrusion is part of a long-term campaign?

keyIdea.text: Organized crime focuses on financial exploitation with repeatable operations; APTs pursue strategic objectives with patient, stealthy techniques and long-term presence.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Organized Crime & APTs
Organized Crime
Focused on monetization through ransomware, credential resale, and data theft. Operations are process-driven and may include service providers and resale markets.
Indicators
  • Mass scanning and bulk phishing campaigns
  • Ransom notes, encrypted file patterns
  • Known crimeware signatures
Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)
Highly resourced and patient attackers pursuing espionage or disruption. Expect stealth, custom tools, and careful reconnaissance.
Indicators
  • Low-volume, targeted access to sensitive systems
  • Use of zero-day exploits or unique payloads
  • Long-lived persistence and lateral movement
Key Takeaway

Distinguish motive and persistence: financial campaigns need different playbooks than long-term espionage to preserve evidence and hunt for latent access.

screens.title: Insider Threats
screens.narratorSegment: Insider threats come from people with authorized access—employees, contractors, or partners—who misuse privileges either intentionally or accidentally. Intentional insiders might steal data for revenge or profit. Negligent insiders may fall for phishing, misconfigure systems, or mishandle credentials, creating openings for external attackers. Detecting insiders is difficult because their actions often look like legitimate use; for example, a privileged user accessing a sensitive folder after hours could be legitimate maintenance or data theft. A concrete example: an employee clicks a well-crafted phishing link and provides credentials, which the attacker then uses; the root cause is an external compromise enabled by insider behavior. Analysts should combine behavioral baselines, access reviews, and context such as job role and recent HR events to assess insider risk. A common misconception is that insider threats are always malicious; in many breaches the insider is the vector without malicious intent. Your investigative focus should include whether access patterns deviate from the expected baseline and whether data access is justified by role. What baseline signals would you establish to detect unusual insider activity? Insider Threats means insider threats can be intentional or negligent; baseline behavior, role context, and access justification are essential to distinguish legitimate use from misuse.. In practical terms, why insiders are uniquely risky and how to detect misuse or negligence.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Insider Risk
keyIdea.text: Insider threats can be intentional or negligent; baseline behavior, role context, and access justification are essential to distinguish legitimate use from misuse.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Insider Threats
Insider Threats Explained
Insider threats may be intentional or accidental. The combination of privileged access and normal-looking activity makes detection challenging.
Examples
  • Disgruntled employee copying sensitive files to a personal device
  • Employee falling for a phishing email and exposing credentials
  • Contractor misconfiguring a storage container allowing public access
Detection Signals
  • Unusual access volume or timing compared to baseline
  • Access to data outside of job responsibilities
  • Use of nonstandard tools or data transfer methods
Common Mistake

Assuming all insiders are malicious. Many incidents begin with negligence; remediation should include training and controls as well as investigation.

screens.title: Attack Vectors Overview
screens.narratorSegment: An attack vector is the method or path an adversary uses to gain initial access or deliver malicious capability into a system. Understanding vectors is essential because different vectors leave distinct evidence and require different detection strategies. Common vectors include phishing, which uses social engineering to harvest credentials or deliver malware; malware delivered via attachments, malicious websites, or removable media; Denial of Service attacks that overwhelm services and obscure other activity; and exploitation of web application vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting. Weak credentials and unpatched software are also vectors because they provide accessible entry points. For an analyst, recognizing the vector helps narrow the hunt — unusual outbound traffic and web requests suggest command-and-control activity from malware, while suspicious email headers and links indicate phishing. A typical misconception is to assume a single vector explains an entire intrusion; more often, attackers chain vectors — for example, phishing for credentials to enable VPN access and lateral movement. Consider how you would combine log sources to validate a suspected vector: email gateway logs, web proxies, endpoint telemetry, and authentication logs together tell a stronger story than any one source alone.

keyIdea.title: Vector Definition
keyIdea.text: Attack vectors are how adversaries enter or move inside systems; identifying them narrows investigation and suggests targeted mitigations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Attack Vectors Overview
Common Vectors
Phishing
Social engineering to harvest credentials or deliver malware; watch headers, domains, and attachments.
Malware
Viruses, ransomware, trojans delivered by email, sites, or removable media; endpoints and network telemetry are key.
DDoS
Traffic floods that deny service; look for volumetric spikes and source distribution.
Web Vulnerabilities
SQL injection and XSS enable data theft or client-side compromise; web logs and input sanitization failures are signals.
Chaining Vectors
Attackers often chain vectors: a phishing email yields credentials, those credentials enable remote access, and an exploited web app provides data exfiltration. Detection must connect these steps across logs.
Key Takeaway

Identifying vectors focuses which logs and controls you examine; assume multiple vectors may be used in sequence.

Check Your Understanding
Name two log sources you would combine to confirm a phishing-to-VPN compromise.

screens.title: Phishing and Spear Phishing
screens.narratorSegment: Phishing is a social engineering vector where attackers impersonate trusted entities to trick users into revealing credentials or executing malware. Spear phishing is a targeted variant that tailors messages to specific individuals to increase success. The attack flow typically starts with reconnaissance: an attacker gathers publicly available information to personalize messages. Next comes delivery: an email, text, or phone call that contains a malicious link or attachment. If the target engages, the attacker obtains credentials or installs a payload, which then enables further phases like lateral movement or data exfiltration. A concrete, chapter-provided scenario shows an employee clicking a fake verification link, submitting credentials to a spoofed login page, and the attacker using those credentials to access VPN and a shared drive. To investigate, correlate email gateway logs, web proxy records for the fake domain, and VPN access logs showing a new source IP or atypical access time. A common misconception is that only naïve users fall for phishing; even well-trained staff can be deceived by convincing spear phishing. Your takeaway should be to seek cross-source evidence: one log alone rarely proves an attack. When you map this sequence to ATT&CK, initial access aligns with T1566 and subsequent steps align with credential use techniques. What single log would you query first to confirm a phishing hypothesis?

keyIdea.text: Phishing begins with social engineering and often leads to credential compromise; investigations must correlate email, web, and authentication logs to build the sequence.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Phishing & Spear Phishing
Attack Steps
Reconnaissance
Gather public info to personalize messages.
Delivery
Email, SMS, or phone with malicious link or attachment.
Credential Capture / Payload
Spoofed login pages or malicious attachments lead to compromise.
Post-Compromise Activity
VPN access, lateral movement, or data exfiltration.
Investigation Checklist
Correlate Logs
Email gateway, web proxy for the spoofed domain, and VPN/authentication logs together trace the attack path.
Map to ATT&CK
Initial Access: T1566 - Phishing; Sub-techniques for attachments or links help refine hunting queries.
Key Takeaway

Phishing is often the start of a multi-step intrusion; confirm by linking email delivery to subsequent authentication events.

screens.title: Malware: Types and Delivery
screens.narratorSegment: Malware is a broad category of malicious software designed to disrupt systems, steal data, or provide unauthorized access. Families include viruses and worms that spread, Trojans that disguise malicious payloads, ransomware that encrypts and holds data for extortion, and spyware that quietly exfiltrates information. Delivery methods vary: email attachments and malicious links are common, as are compromised websites and removable media. Attackers may also drop custom backdoors once access is established so they can return later. When investigating malware, endpoint telemetry, file hashes, process trees, and network connections are primary evidence sources. A concrete example: a user opens an email attachment that runs a trojan which establishes an outbound encrypted channel to attacker infrastructure. Misconception: not all malware shows obvious symptoms like crashes or pop-ups; advanced malware often operates stealthily. For defense, focus on layered controls — email filtering, endpoint detection, timely patching, and network monitoring — because no single control stops every family. Ask yourself which telemetry sources you would prioritize to detect a stealthy backdoor that uses standard web protocols for command and control. narration.text: Malware is a broad category of malicious software designed to disrupt systems, steal data, or provide unauthorized access. Families include viruses and worms that spread, Trojans that disguise malicious payloads, ransomware that encrypts and holds data for extortion, and spyware that quietly exfiltrates information. Delivery methods vary: email attachments and malicious links are common, as are compromised websites and removable media. Attackers may also drop custom backdoors once access is established so they can return later. When investigating malware, endpoint telemetry, file hashes, process trees, and network connections are primary evidence sources. A concrete example: a user opens an email attachment that runs a trojan which establishes an outbound encrypted channel to attacker infrastructure. Misconception: not all malware shows obvious symptoms like crashes or pop-ups; advanced malware often operates stealthily. For defense, focus on layered controls — email filtering, endpoint detection, timely patching, and network monitoring — because no single control stops every family. Ask yourself which telemetry sources you would prioritize to detect a stealthy backdoor that uses standard web protocols for command and control. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Malware: Types & Delivery
Malware Families
  • Virus/Worm: self-replicating code that spreads to other systems.
  • Trojan: disguised payload that enables initial access or backdoor.
  • Ransomware: encrypts data to demand payment.
  • Spyware: stealthy data collection and exfiltration.
Delivery Channels
  • Email attachments and malicious links
  • Compromised websites and drive-by downloads
  • Removable media and supply chain compromises
  • Post-compromise installation of bespoke backdoors
Common Mistake

Expecting visible symptoms. Many modern malware families are stealthy to avoid detection and persist long-term.

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS)
screens.narratorSegment: Denial of Service attacks aim to make a service unavailable by overwhelming it with traffic or resource demands. Distributed Denial of Service, or DDoS, uses many sources to make mitigation harder. From an analyst's perspective, the investigation must distinguish between legitimate traffic spikes — for example, a marketing campaign driving many users — and malicious floods. Key indicators of DDoS include sudden, high-volume increases in requests from diverse or spoofed sources, repeated requests to a specific endpoint, and saturated network or application logs. A practical approach is to correlate network telemetry with application logs and business calendars; if a traffic surge is not aligned with expected activity, treat it as suspicious. Misconception: assuming every volumetric spike is an attack; context matters. Also, DDoS can be a diversion tactic while attackers pursue other objectives, so check for simultaneous anomalies like authentication failures or new administrative sessions. Your response options vary from rate-limiting and filtering to engaging upstream providers and focusing on application-layer protections. How would you assemble evidence to distinguish a high-traffic product launch from a coordinated DDoS? Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS)
DDoS Overview
Indicators
  • High request rate across many source IPs
  • Sustained traffic spikes not tied to business events
  • Service errors and resource saturation
Mitigation Tactics
  • Rate limiting and filtering at edge
  • Engage upstream providers or CDN protections
  • Focus on application-layer controls for targeted floods
Investigation Tip

Always check for concurrent anomalies. DDoS may be a diversion for lateral movement or credential misuse elsewhere in your environment.

screens.title: Web Application Vulnerabilities — SQLi & XSS
screens.narratorSegment: Web application vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting exploit poor input validation to run attacker-controlled code or queries. S Q L injection allows an attacker to insert malicious S Q L into application inputs to read or modify database content. Cross-site scripting enables attackers to inject client-side scripts that run in other users' browsers, potentially stealing session tokens or delivering malicious payloads. A concrete detection example: a spike in unusual query parameters combined with database errors and abnormal data access patterns may point to S Q L injection attempts. For XSS, monitoring for unusual scripts in user-submitted content and complaints of redirected sessions can help detect exploitation. Analysts should pair web logs, application error logs, and database audit trails to build a case. A common misconception is that only legacy applications have these flaws; modern apps can be vulnerable without proper input sanitization. Remediation often requires code fixes and input validation, but in the interim web application firewalls and strict content security policies reduce exposure. Which logs would you prioritize to validate a suspected S Q L injection attempt?

keyIdea.title: Web Vulnerabilities
keyIdea.text: SQLi and XSS exploit input validation failures; combine web, application, and database logs to detect and validate exploitation attempts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SQLi & XSS
SQL Injection
Attackers inject SQL into input fields to manipulate queries and access or modify data beyond intended privileges.
Detection Signals
  • Unexpected SQL syntax in query parameters
  • Database errors correlated with specific inputs
  • Unusual data export patterns
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Attackers inject client-side scripts that run in other users' browsers, enabling session theft or forced actions.
Detection Signals
  • Script content in user-submitted fields
  • Unexpected redirects or cookie exfiltration
  • User reports of strange behavior after visiting pages
Mitigation

Apply input validation and parameterized queries for SQLi, and use content security policies and output encoding to reduce XSS risk.

screens.title: Weak Credentials, Unpatched Systems, and Misconfigurations
screens.narratorSegment: Weak passwords, unpatched software, and misconfigurations are among the simplest but most exploited vectors. Attackers scan for exposed services and try common or reused credentials. Unpatched systems present known vulnerabilities that can be exploited with readily available exploit code. Misconfigurations, like open storage containers or overly permissive access controls, offer direct access without technical exploits. These internal vectors are sometimes overlooked because they seem mundane, yet they are high-value for attackers: stolen credentials let attackers impersonate legitimate users and move laterally. A practical example is an attacker using harvested credentials from phishing to authenticate to a VPN and then exploiting an unpatched file server to install persistent access. Analysts should monitor for failed login bursts, unusual privileged account access, and indicators of known CVEs against inventory records. A common misconception is that only exotic attacks matter; in reality, many incidents start with trivial misconfigurations. The key defensive steps are inventory, patch prioritization, password hygiene, and access minimization. What monitoring rule would help surface an attacker using valid credentials from an unusual location? content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Credentials, Patching & Configs
Weak Credentials
Reused or weak passwords allow brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks; privileged account misuse amplifies impact.
Detection Tips
  • Monitor failed login rates and geographic anomalies
  • Watch for impossible travel or new device enrollments
Patches & Misconfigurations
Unpatched CVEs and incorrect settings provide easy entry. Regular inventory and prioritized patching reduce attack surface.
Mitigation
  • Maintain software inventory and prioritize high-severity patches
  • Use least privilege and review access policies regularly
Key Takeaway

Don’t ignore basic hygiene: credentials, patches, and configurations are often the simplest path for attackers and are highly preventable.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts summarize what you should remember when analyzing threats. First: classify the actor by capability and motive — script kiddies, hacktivists, organized crime, APTs, and insiders each imply different urgency and evidence needs. Second: identify the vector — phishing, malware, DDoS, or web vulnerabilities — and gather corroborating logs from mail gateways, endpoints, network telemetry, and application or database logs to build a complete chain of activity. Third: reason from motivation — a financially motivated actor will likely target monetizable data, while espionage-driven actors target sensitive intellectual property or long-term access. Together, these concepts—actor, vector, and motivation—help you prioritize, hunt, and recommend mitigations. A practical habit is to map observed activity to MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs to standardize reporting and search patterns. As you wrap up this chapter, ask yourself how each alert you review would be different if the suspected actor were an APT versus a script kiddie. That contrast will sharpen your triage and incident decisions.

screens.title: Key Concepts — MITRE ATT&CK & Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: The MITRE ATT&CK framework gives you a common language to describe attacker behavior, turning narrative steps into searchable technique IDs. First: use ATT&CK tactics to structure your timeline — for example, Initial Access followed by Execution and Persistence — so you can communicate where activity sits in an attack lifecycle. Second: when you identify a step such as phishing, map it to a specific technique like T1566 and sub-techniques such as T1566.001 for spearphishing attachments; these IDs let you search logs consistently and compare findings across incidents. Third: use ATT&CK mapping to evaluate defensive coverage — knowing which techniques attackers use helps you assess gaps in detection and prioritize mitigations. In the phishing-to-data-access scenario, you can map the email to T1566, credential usage to valid accounts techniques, and data access to collection techniques. A helpful habit is to record technique IDs in your incident reports; they make your findings actionable and reproducible. What technique IDs would you record for a phishing email that led to VPN access and file retrieval?

ATT&CK Mapping Essentials
Structure Timelines
Use ATT&CK tactics to anchor where each event occurs in the attack lifecycle.
Use Technique IDs
Map steps to IDs like T1566 to standardize searches and reports.
Assess Coverage
Compare detected techniques against your controls to find gaps and prioritize defenses.

Phishing → T1566; Spearphishing Attachment → T1566.001; Valid Accounts for later VPN use → T1078. Use these IDs in hunt queries and reports.

fullNarratorScript:
To defend effectively, you must first understand the people and methods behind attacks. In this lesson you will build a mental model for classifying threat actors — from casual script kiddies to sophisticated advanced persistent threats — and learn the common vectors they use, such as phishing, malware, and web application exploitation. You will also learn how attacker motivations, whether financial, political, or opportunistic, shape what they target and when they act. Finally, we will introduce the MITRE ATT&CK framework as a practical language for mapping adversary behavior to tactics and techniques. This orientation matters because detection and response choices change when you know the likely adversary and their motives. For example, an incident that looks like credential theft from a phishing email will be triaged differently if you suspect a nation-state espionage group versus a financially motivated gang. By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify actor categories, link them to likely vectors, and begin mapping observed activity to ATT&CK techniques so you can prioritize investigations and recommend mitigations. Consider what pattern of behavior would make you treat an alert as urgent versus informational.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to categorize threat actors by capability and intent, identify common attack vectors, explain attacker motivations, and apply the MITRE ATT&CK framework to real incidents. First, you will learn to distinguish simple attackers who use off‑the‑shelf tools from sophisticated, well‑resourced groups whose goals are espionage or infrastructure disruption. Second, you will map vectors such as phishing, malware delivery, DDoS, and web application exploits to likely outcomes so you can recognize early indicators. Third, you will reason from motivation — for example, understanding that financially motivated groups prioritize data capable of monetization — and use that insight to prioritize. Finally, you will learn to read ATT&CK tactics and techniques and use them to frame hunt queries and incident timelines. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify what you have learned by mapping a scenario to ATT&CK entries and selecting appropriate mitigations. These skills matter because they make your detection more accurate and your response more effective. Think about a recent alert you investigated: which of these objectives would have changed how you triaged it?

This second objectives page focuses on observable outcomes you should demonstrate after practice. You will learn to extract indicators that point to specific vectors: for example, how suspicious mail headers, unusual referral domains, and credential use patterns signal phishing followed by account misuse. You will practice mapping scenario steps to ATT&CK technique IDs so your investigation reports use a consistent taxonomy. You will also learn to prioritize alerts: treat activity from high-capability actors and those aligned to espionage or infrastructure disruption as high priority, while low-skill opportunistic probes may be monitored until additional evidence appears. A common misconception is to equate volume with severity; a low-volume, targeted intrusion from a sophisticated actor can be more dangerous than a high-volume noisy scan. Practical verification includes mapping a phishing-to-data-access scenario to at least three ATT&CK techniques and explaining why each technique applies. These outcomes align with CySA+ objectives and will improve your detection accuracy and decision-making when incidents arise.

Threat actors are individuals or groups who carry out cyberattacks, and classifying them helps you anticipate method and motive. At the low end you have script kiddies: unsophisticated users who run pre-built tools to exploit known weaknesses, often seeking recognition rather than strategic gain. Hacktivists are ideologically motivated and select symbolic targets to make a statement or disrupt visibility. Organized crime groups are financially driven; they adopt professional practices like ransomware campaigns, data theft, and resale of stolen data, and often have processes resembling a business. Advanced Persistent Threats, or APTs, are highly resourced groups—sometimes nation-state sponsored—with long-term objectives such as espionage or critical infrastructure disruption; they use custom tools and remain stealthy for extended periods. Insider threats are different because they originate from someone with authorized access; harm may be intentional or due to negligence. A useful example: an alert showing a low-skill defacement of a public blog likely indicates a script kiddie, whereas covert exfiltration of R&D from privileged accounts suggests an APT. A common misconception is to treat all breaches the same; in reality, your containment, evidence preservation, and notification decisions should reflect the actor profile. What indicators would make you suspect an insider versus an external actor?

Understanding the differences between script kiddies and hacktivists helps you decide how much effort to invest in containment and follow-up. Script kiddies are typically curious or seeking notoriety; they use publicly available tools and target low-hanging fruit such as poorly secured blogs or consumer devices. Their activity tends to be noisy and opportunistic, and indicators include well-known exploit signatures, repeated scanning, and generic payloads. Hacktivists are motivated by ideology. Their attacks are chosen for symbolic impact and may focus on government sites or corporations linked to particular causes; they might also deface pages or leak documents to gain attention. Although hacktivists are not always highly sophisticated, their motives can lead to targeted timing or social-engineering that increases impact. A practical example: a visible defacement on a public website is likely a hacktivist or script kiddie depending on messaging — ideological slogans point to hacktivism, while random brags suggest a script kiddie. A misconception is assuming all ideological attacks are low skill; some hacktivist operations use careful reconnaissance and timing. When you spot early signs like unique slogans or targeted timing, escalate your analysis to look for coordinated messaging and wider campaign indicators. How would your log search change if you suspected ideological motives?

Organized crime and APTs differ in motive and often in methods, but both can be highly capable and dangerous. Organized crime groups are primarily financially motivated. They develop operations to monetize stolen data, run ransomware campaigns, or sell access. Their activity is often pragmatic: repeatable processes, supply chains for crimeware, and a focus on return on investment. APTs, on the other hand, are frequently sponsored by nation-states or extremely well‑resourced organizations. Their objectives include espionage, intellectual property theft, or disruption of critical infrastructure. APT campaigns are characterized by patient reconnaissance, use of zero-day exploits or bespoke malware, and long-term persistence. A concrete example: an incident that shows staged credential harvesting followed by quiet lateral movement aimed at specific research databases suggests APT activity, while mass ransomware deployment across many victims points to organized crime. A common misconception is that APTs always use exotic tools; sometimes they blend commodity malware with custom tooling and careful operational security. Your response differs: APT suspicion demands comprehensive evidence preservation, intelligence sharing, and a broader hunt for lateral activity. Ask yourself: what signs would convince you that an intrusion is part of a long-term campaign?

Insider threats come from people with authorized access—employees, contractors, or partners—who misuse privileges either intentionally or accidentally. Intentional insiders might steal data for revenge or profit. Negligent insiders may fall for phishing, misconfigure systems, or mishandle credentials, creating openings for external attackers. Detecting insiders is difficult because their actions often look like legitimate use; for example, a privileged user accessing a sensitive folder after hours could be legitimate maintenance or data theft. A concrete example: an employee clicks a well-crafted phishing link and provides credentials, which the attacker then uses; the root cause is an external compromise enabled by insider behavior. Analysts should combine behavioral baselines, access reviews, and context such as job role and recent HR events to assess insider risk. A common misconception is that insider threats are always malicious; in many breaches the insider is the vector without malicious intent. Your investigative focus should include whether access patterns deviate from the expected baseline and whether data access is justified by role. What baseline signals would you establish to detect unusual insider activity? Insider Threats means insider threats can be intentional or negligent; baseline behavior, role context, and access justification are essential to distinguish legitimate use from misuse.. In practical terms, why insiders are uniquely risky and how to detect misuse or negligence.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An attack vector is the method or path an adversary uses to gain initial access or deliver malicious capability into a system. Understanding vectors is essential because different vectors leave distinct evidence and require different detection strategies. Common vectors include phishing, which uses social engineering to harvest credentials or deliver malware; malware delivered via attachments, malicious websites, or removable media; Denial of Service attacks that overwhelm services and obscure other activity; and exploitation of web application vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting. Weak credentials and unpatched software are also vectors because they provide accessible entry points. For an analyst, recognizing the vector helps narrow the hunt — unusual outbound traffic and web requests suggest command-and-control activity from malware, while suspicious email headers and links indicate phishing. A typical misconception is to assume a single vector explains an entire intrusion; more often, attackers chain vectors — for example, phishing for credentials to enable VPN access and lateral movement. Consider how you would combine log sources to validate a suspected vector: email gateway logs, web proxies, endpoint telemetry, and authentication logs together tell a stronger story than any one source alone.

Phishing is a social engineering vector where attackers impersonate trusted entities to trick users into revealing credentials or executing malware. Spear phishing is a targeted variant that tailors messages to specific individuals to increase success. A common misconception is that only naïve users fall for phishing; even well-trained staff can be deceived by convincing spear phishing. Your takeaway should be to seek cross-source evidence: one log alone rarely proves an attack. When you map this sequence to ATT&CK, initial access aligns with T1566 and subsequent steps align with credential use techniques. What single log would you query first to confirm a phishing hypothesis?

Weak passwords, unpatched software, and misconfigurations are among the simplest but most exploited vectors. Attackers scan for exposed services and try common or reused credentials. Unpatched systems present known vulnerabilities that can be exploited with readily available exploit code. Misconfigurations, like open storage containers or overly permissive access controls, offer direct access without technical exploits. These internal vectors are sometimes overlooked because they seem mundane, yet they are high-value for attackers: stolen credentials let attackers impersonate legitimate users and move laterally. A practical example is an attacker using harvested credentials from phishing to authenticate to a VPN and then exploiting an unpatched file server to install persistent access. Analysts should monitor for failed login bursts, unusual privileged account access, and indicators of known CVEs against inventory records. A common misconception is that only exotic attacks matter; in reality, many incidents start with trivial misconfigurations. The key defensive steps are inventory, patch prioritization, password hygiene, and access minimization. These three core concepts summarize what you should remember when analyzing threats. First: classify the actor by capability and motive — script kiddies, hacktivists, organized crime, APTs, and insiders each imply different urgency and evidence needs. Second: identify the vector — phishing, malware, DDoS, or web vulnerabilities — and gather corroborating logs from mail gateways, endpoints, network telemetry, and application or database logs to build a complete chain of activity. Third: reason from motivation — a financially motivated actor will likely target monetizable data, while espionage-driven actors target sensitive intellectual property or long-term access. Together, these concepts—actor, vector, and motivation—help you prioritize, hunt, and recommend mitigations. A practical habit is to map observed activity to MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs to standardize reporting and search patterns. That contrast will sharpen your triage and incident decisions.

The MITRE ATT&CK framework gives you a common language to describe attacker behavior, turning narrative steps into searchable technique IDs. First: use ATT&CK tactics to structure your timeline — for example, Initial Access followed by Execution and Persistence — so you can communicate where activity sits in an attack lifecycle. Second: when you identify a step such as phishing, map it to a specific technique like T1566 and sub-techniques such as T1566.001 for spearphishing attachments; these IDs let you search logs consistently and compare findings across incidents. Third: use ATT&CK mapping to evaluate defensive coverage — knowing which techniques attackers use helps you assess gaps in detection and prioritize mitigations. In the phishing-to-data-access scenario, you can map the email to T1566, credential usage to valid accounts techniques, and data access to collection techniques. A helpful habit is to record technique IDs in your incident reports; they make your findings actionable and reproducible.
